newsitem.title: USA: Four Democrats oppose change to U.S. bank law.
newsitem.headline: Four Democrats oppose change to U.S. bank law.

text.p: Four Democratic senators wrote Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin Wednesday to oppose proposals they said would weaken the 1991 Truth in Savings Act.
"We want to alert you to our opposition to proposals" that would weaken the act, said Patrick Leahy of Vermont, Bill Bradley of New Jersey, Paul Simon of Illinois and Paul Wellstone of Minnesota.

The senators were concerned the proposals, which cleared the Senate Banking Committee last year, could be included in banking reforms expected to be attached to a huge government spending bill for fiscal 1997, an aide to Leahy said. The bill is slated for action before Congress adjourns for the year.
The changes to the Truth in Savings Act were only one portion of banking reforms and were proposed by Senate Banking Committee chairman Alfonse D'Amato (R-New York) and others.

"The act requires banks to advertise yields on deposit accounts in identical fashion so that consumers can instantly compare one bank's offering with another," the senators said in their letter. They said the act also gives consumers information about fees charged and interest paid.

Consumers Union, which released the letter, said that if the bill is passed, the banking industry would have the "green light to resort to the same kinds of deceptive promotional gimmicks they used in the past to make their accounts look more attractive than they really were."
The measure would be included in a bill that would involve banks in a process to help increase the solidity of insurance for thrifts.
"Banks argue they should be able to weaken (the consumer protections) in response for stepping up their contribution" to the thrift fund, Consumers Union said.
No one from the American Bankers Association was immediately available for comment.
